title: WHY DID PAUL SAY TO STOP ASSOCIATING WITH SOMEONE WHO CLAIMS TO FOLLOW JESUS BUT REFUSES TO TURN AWAY FROM SEXUAL SIN?
paragraphs: WHY DID PAUL SAY TO STOP ASSOCIATING WITH SOMEONE WHO CLAIMS TO FOLLOW JESUS BUT REFUSES TO TURN AWAY FROM SEXUAL SIN?
The Warning Most Churches Are Afraid to Preach, the Truth Many Christians Misunderstand, and the Heartbreaking Reason Biblical Love Sometimes Requires Walking Away.
“I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators.” — 1 Corinthians 5:9 (KJV)
Imagine sitting across from someone you love.
Someone who knows the Scriptures. Someone who raises their hands during worship. Someone who says, “Jesus is Lord,” and perhaps has said those words for years.
But there is something you cannot ignore anymore.
They are openly living in sexual sin.
Not because they stumbled once and are desperately trying to get back up.
Not because they are struggling with temptation and crying out to God for deliverance.
But because they have decided that what Scripture calls sin is no longer something they need to repent of.
And when someone lovingly confronts them, they respond:
“Only God can judge me.”
“Jesus ate with sinners.”
“Stop being so religious.”
“God knows my heart.”
Then comes the question that can tear a Christian friendship, a family, or even an entire church apart.
What does love require you to do when someone claims to belong to Jesus but refuses to listen to Jesus?
Do you stay silent because you are afraid of losing them?
Do you keep affirming their choices because you do not want to appear judgmental?
Or is there a moment when continuing to act as though nothing is wrong becomes a form of spiritual dishonesty?
The Apostle Paul answered that question in one of the most uncomfortable passages in the New Testament.
And before you decide his words sound too harsh, you need to understand something.
Paul was not writing because he hated sinners.
He was writing because he understood what unrepentant sin could do to a soul, to a church, and to the credibility of the Gospel.
But there is another truth hidden in the context that makes this passage even more powerful.
The same Paul who commanded the church to remove an unrepentant person also taught that a repentant sinner must be welcomed back with love.
That changes how we read everything.
Because this is not ultimately a story about who deserves to be thrown away.
It is about what happens when a church stops taking sin seriously—and what grace looks like when someone finally comes home.
To understand Paul's warning, we must return to Corinth.
The church in Corinth was surrounded by a culture where sexual immorality was widespread. Yet Paul was not primarily concerned that sinful behavior existed outside the church.
He was confronting something far more disturbing.
Inside the Christian community, a man was involved in a sexual relationship with his father's wife.
Paul described the situation in 1 Corinthians 5:1, using the Greek expression γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν (gynaika tina tou patros echein), meaning that someone had his father's wife.
The wording does not establish every detail of the relationship, but it clearly describes a grave sexual violation.
And the church's response?
Instead of mourning, they were arrogant.
Paul writes:
Think about that.
The scandal was not only what one man was doing.
The scandal was that the church had become comfortable with it.
They had confused tolerance with maturity.
They had mistaken the absence of correction for the presence of love.
And Paul was telling them that their spiritual pride had blinded them to the danger.
There is something terrifying about a church that can still sing about holiness while refusing to confront serious, unrepentant sin within its own fellowship.
Not because the church is supposed to be filled with perfect people.
It never was.
But because the church is supposed to be a community where sinners are being transformed by the grace of Jesus Christ.
And transformation becomes impossible to celebrate honestly when repentance is treated as optional.
Then Paul writes the words that many Christians struggle to understand.
“I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators.” — 1 Corinthians 5:9 (KJV)
The Greek expression translated “to company with” is συναναμίγνυσθαι (synanamignysthai).
It carries the sense of associating or mixing together with others.
But here is the crucial detail.
Paul immediately explains that he does not mean Christians must stop associating with every sexually immoral person in the world.
He writes:
Read that again.
Paul is explicitly rejecting the idea that Christians should isolate themselves from unbelievers who live contrary to biblical morality.
If that were the standard, Christians would have to leave the world entirely.
How could we evangelize?
How could we show compassion?
How could we serve our neighbors?
How could we follow Jesus, who was criticized for welcoming tax collectors and sinners?
Jesus did not avoid people because their lives were broken.
He came to seek and save the lost.
And His church must never forget that.
But then Paul makes a distinction.

“But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.” — 1 Corinthians 5:11 (KJV)
The Greek expression ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος (adelphos onomazomenos) refers to someone who is called or identified as a brother.
In this context, Paul is speaking about a person who professes membership in the Christian community.
And the distinction matters enormously.
Paul is not saying:
“Reject anyone who struggles with sexual temptation.”
He is not saying:
“Abandon every believer who has fallen.”
He is not saying:
“Treat everyone with a painful past as spiritually contaminated.”

He is confronting the serious problem of someone claiming Christian identity while continuing in conduct plainly contrary to the Gospel, without repentance, and while the church treats the situation as acceptable.
The issue is not simply that a sinner exists among sinners.
The issue is that someone is claiming the authority of Christ while refusing His call to repentance.
And before anyone uses this passage as permission to become cruel, we need to remember something.
Paul did not limit his warning to sexual immorality.
He also named greed, idolatry, abusive speech, drunkenness, and exploitation.
The Greek word πλεονέκτης (pleonektēs) refers to a greedy or covetous person.
The word λοίδορος (loidoros) refers to someone who reviles or abuses others verbally.
The word ἅρπαξ (harpax) describes someone who takes advantage of others through robbery or extortion.
This should make every self-righteous reader uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to condemn sexual sin while excusing greed.
Easy to expose adultery while overlooking cruelty.
Easy to confront another person's immoral relationship while ignoring our own dishonest business practices, abusive words, or exploitation of vulnerable people.
Paul did not give the church permission to choose a favorite category of sinner to condemn.
He called the church to integrity.
And integrity begins when we allow Scripture to examine us before we use it to examine someone else.
Jesus Himself warned against trying to remove a speck from another person's eye while ignoring the plank in our own (Matthew 7:3–5).
That does not mean Christians must never correct anyone.
It means correction must begin with humility.
Because there is a difference between someone who is broken over sin and someone who is determined to defend it.
Imagine two believers.
One has fallen into sexual sin.
They are ashamed. They know they have disobeyed God. They are not proud of what happened.
They confess it.
They ask for prayer.
They seek accountability.
They may still be struggling, and the road to restoration may be difficult.
But their heart is turning toward Christ.
Now imagine another person.
They openly continue in sexual immorality.
They refuse biblical correction.
They insist that repentance is unnecessary.
They demand that the church affirm what Scripture condemns.
Both people need Jesus.
Both need grace.
Both need truth.
But their responses to that truth are not the same.
Repentance does not mean a person has already become perfect. It means they are turning toward God rather than making peace with their rebellion.
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It concerns a change of mind and heart that involves turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what you were doing.
It is not simply crying because consequences arrived.
It is a genuine turning that, over time, bears fruit in changed conduct.
And that is why Paul takes unrepentant sin so seriously.
He understands that a person can become so accustomed to defending sin that correction begins to feel like hatred.
Sometimes the very voice trying to awaken us becomes the voice we most desperately want to silence.
Have you ever experienced that?
Someone confronted you with a truth you did not want to hear.
Your first instinct was to explain yourself.
To justify your behavior.
To remind them of their own failures.
But later, alone with God, you realized something painful.
They had not been trying to destroy you.
They had been trying to reach you.
Not every confrontation is loving, and not every accusation is true.
But when correction is grounded in Scripture, established facts, humility, and genuine concern, rejecting it simply because it hurts can be spiritually dangerous.
Proverbs 27:6 says:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.” (KJV)
Sometimes the friend who refuses to flatter us is the friend who loves us enough to risk losing our approval.
And sometimes the person who always tells us what we want to hear is helping us remain exactly where we should not be.
This brings us to Paul's most difficult instruction.
He tells the Corinthians not to associate with the unrepentant professing believer, adding, “with such an one no not to eat.”
What does that mean?
In the ancient world, sharing meals often expressed fellowship, hospitality, acceptance, and social solidarity.
Paul's instruction was a serious restriction of ordinary fellowship with someone whose public, persistent conduct contradicted their Christian profession.
The passage also concerns the church's responsibility to remove such a person from recognized fellowship.
Christians differ over the precise application of the meal restriction today, including its relationship to ordinary social contact and participation in the Lord's Supper.
But the central point is unmistakable.
The church must not communicate spiritual approval where Scripture calls for repentance.
This does not authorize harassment.
It does not authorize humiliation.
It does not authorize physical abuse, threats, or public campaigns to destroy someone's reputation.
It does not require abandoning basic kindness, refusing necessary care, or treating a person as less than human.
And it must never be used to protect abusive leaders, silence victims, or punish someone for reporting wrongdoing.
Biblical church discipline requires truth, fairness, pastoral wisdom, and appropriate accountability.
Jesus described a process of correction in Matthew 18:15–17 that begins with personal engagement and seeks to regain the person.
Paul's own instruction in Galatians 6:1 is equally important:
“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” (KJV)
Notice that word.
Restore.
Not humiliate.
Not entertain the congregation with someone's failure.
Not use another person's sin as an opportunity to feel morally superior.
Restore.
And Paul adds that those doing the restoring must watch themselves.
Because the moment you begin to believe you are incapable of falling is often the moment you become dangerously vulnerable to pride.
Church discipline is not a license for the righteous to celebrate the downfall of the unrighteous.
It is a sober responsibility carried out by people who know they themselves survive only by grace.
And the deeper we enter 1 Corinthians 5, the more clearly we see why Paul was so urgent.
He asks:
“Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?” — 1 Corinthians 5:6 (KJV)
Leaven was commonly used as an image of something that spreads through dough.
Paul uses it to warn that tolerated, unrepentant sin can affect the entire community.
When a church publicly normalizes conduct contrary to its own confession, the damage rarely remains confined to one person.
Others begin to wonder whether obedience matters.
Those fighting temptation may become discouraged.
Those wounded by similar behavior may feel abandoned.
And the church's testimony becomes confused.
But Paul does not stop with the warning.
He points to Christ.
“For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.” — 1 Corinthians 5:7 (KJV)
There it is.
The center of the entire passage.
Not the scandal.
Not the discipline.
Not the church's reputation.
Jesus Christ, our Passover sacrifice.
Paul connects the church's call to holiness with the saving work of Christ.
In the Passover story, Israel's deliverance was grounded in God's saving intervention.
Paul now identifies Christ as the fulfillment of that sacrificial imagery.
The church does not pursue holiness to purchase redemption.
The church pursues holiness because redemption has come through Jesus.
We do not repent so that we can make the cross powerful.
We repent because the crucified and risen Christ is worthy of our allegiance.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us and teaches us to turn from ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
And this is where the message becomes personal.
Because perhaps you have been reading this entire article thinking about someone else.
A friend.
A former partner.
A church member.
A leader.
A relative.
Someone whose choices have troubled you.
But what if the Holy Spirit is also inviting you to examine your own life?
What if the sin you have learned to explain away is the very thing God is calling you to surrender?
Perhaps nobody knows about the relationship.
Perhaps the messages are hidden.
Perhaps the pornography has become a private habit.
Perhaps you have been crossing boundaries you once promised yourself you would never cross.
Perhaps you keep telling yourself that you will repent when the timing becomes convenient.
After the next meeting.
After the next weekend.
After one more night.
After the relationship becomes easier to leave.
But there is a question that deserves an honest answer.
What if the most dangerous thing about your sin is no longer that you are committing it, but that you are beginning to feel comfortable defending it?
Sin often becomes easier to tolerate before it becomes easier to abandon.
The conscience grows quieter.
Excuses grow more convincing.
And the distance between what we profess and how we live becomes something we learn to manage rather than something we bring before God.
Yet even here, the Gospel speaks.
Jesus did not come to save people who had successfully concealed every failure.
He came to save sinners.
The cross is not reserved for people with respectable histories.
The resurrection is not good news only for those whose reputations survived.
Christ offers forgiveness to those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance hopeful.
Because you are not being invited to confess your sin before a Savior who is unwilling to forgive.
You are being invited to bring the truth into the presence of the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
And perhaps that is why Paul's warning is so severe.
He knows the consequences of remaining in spiritual self-deception.
In 1 Corinthians 5:5, Paul speaks of delivering the offender to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, “that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.”
This is a difficult verse, and Christians have debated the exact meaning of “destruction of the flesh.”

The language likely involves removing the person from the protective fellowship of the church and exposing them to the severe consequences of their rebellion, though the precise nature of those consequences remains disputed.
But one part of Paul's stated purpose is unmistakable.
“That the spirit may be saved.”
Even in this severe disciplinary action, Paul expresses a saving purpose.
The goal is not simply to make the person suffer.
It is to confront the seriousness of sin in the hope of ultimate salvation.
That is a radically different motive from revenge.
And it should shape every church that claims to follow Paul's instruction.
If discipline is administered with delight in someone's humiliation, something has gone wrong.
If correction becomes an instrument of control, something has gone wrong.
If the congregation cares more about protecting its public image than restoring a soul, something has gone wrong.
The church must take sin seriously.
But it must also take grace seriously.
And grace does not disappear when someone falls.
Now comes one of the most beautiful possibilities in this entire biblical conversation.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul speaks of a person who has received sufficient punishment from the majority and now needs forgiveness, comfort, and renewed love.
He writes:
Then he urges them to reaffirm their love.
Some interpreters believe this person may have been the offender discussed in 1 Corinthians 5.
Others believe the passages concern different situations.
Scripture does not establish the identification conclusively, so we should not present it as certain.
But regardless of whether the individuals are the same, the principle is clear.
Paul did not believe that church discipline should become permanent rejection when repentance called for restoration.
The same apostle who demanded accountability also demanded forgiveness and comfort.
He understood that excessive sorrow could crush a person.
He understood that discipline without a pathway toward restoration could become spiritually destructive.
And he understood that a church must know not only when to confront sin, but also when to open its arms to the repentant.
Can you imagine how different some Christian communities would be if they took both responsibilities equally seriously?
Imagine a church where serious sin was not excused.
But neither was a repentant person forever defined by their worst decision.
Imagine leaders who confronted wrongdoing without cruelty.
Imagine believers who confessed their failures without fear that repentance would become a lifetime sentence of public shame.
Imagine a community where truth was never sacrificed for popularity, and mercy was never sacrificed for appearances.
That is the kind of community the Gospel calls us toward.
Not a community without sinners.
A community of sinners being transformed by Jesus.
And there is an image from the ministry of Christ that captures this tension beautifully.
In John 8:1–11, a woman accused of adultery is brought before Jesus.
Her accusers are eager to condemn her.
Jesus exposes their hypocrisy.
And when the confrontation ends, He says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11 (KJV)

A textual note matters here: the account in John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and its textual history is disputed. It should therefore be read with awareness of that issue rather than treated as an uncontested textual witness.
Nevertheless, the two themes expressed in the account—mercy toward sinners and a call to leave sin—are abundantly supported elsewhere in the New Testament.
Jesus receives sinners.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus forgives sinners.
Jesus transforms sinners.
We must never use His compassion to erase His holiness.
And we must never use His holiness to erase His compassion.
This is why Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 5 cannot be reduced to “cut off everyone who sins.”
If that were the message, no Christian could remain in fellowship.
Romans 3:23 tells us that all have sinned.
The difference is not between people who need grace and people who do not.
We all need grace.
The question in 1 Corinthians 5 is whether the church will affirm someone in a serious, openly unrepentant pattern of conduct that contradicts their profession of faith.
That is not the same as a believer confessing sin, seeking help, and fighting to walk in obedience.
And we must be careful not to pretend we can see every secret motive of another person's heart.
God knows the heart perfectly.
We do not.
Churches must assess observable conduct and responses to correction with humility, patience, reliable evidence, and biblical wisdom.
They must also recognize that a person may be trapped in abuse, coercion, or exploitation rather than freely choosing wrongdoing.
Such situations require protection and care, not careless accusations.
And even when discipline is warranted, Christians are still commanded to love.
Paul himself says in 2 Thessalonians 3:15, concerning a different disciplinary situation:
“Yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.” (KJV)
The contexts are not identical, but the instruction reveals the pastoral spirit that should accompany correction.
Do not make an enemy out of the person you hope to restore.
Do not confuse boundaries with hatred.
Do not confuse compassion with approval.
And do not confuse someone's present refusal to repent with proof that God's grace can never reach them.
Some of the most powerful testimonies begin with a person who once resisted every warning.
Someone who mocked correction.
Someone who defended their sin.
Someone who walked away from fellowship.
And then, through circumstances we could never have orchestrated, God brought them to repentance.
We cannot guarantee that outcome for every individual.
But we can pray for it.
We can leave the door open to genuine restoration.
We can refuse to compromise truth while refusing to abandon hope.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that sinners are beyond rescue.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
That is the foundation.
Not moral superiority.
Not religious performance.
Not a spotless public image.
Christ crucified and risen.
And when He saves a person, He does not merely give them a new label.
He calls them into a new life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
That transformation may involve painful confession.
It may require ending a sinful relationship.
It may require accountability, restitution, professional support where appropriate, and rebuilding trust over time.
It may mean accepting consequences that forgiveness does not automatically remove.
But it also means the past does not have to be the final chapter.
That is what makes grace so extraordinary.
It does not need to pretend the scandal never happened.
It tells the truth about the scandal.
Then it points to a Savior greater than the scandal.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by pretending rebellion is obedience.
Not by teaching us to celebrate what Christ died to redeem us from.
But by forgiving, cleansing, and transforming those who turn to Him.
So what should you do if someone you love claims to be a Christian while openly persisting in sexual immorality?
Begin with prayer and humility.
Examine your own heart.
Make sure you understand the facts.
Speak the truth privately and lovingly where appropriate.
Encourage repentance, accountability, and pastoral help.
Do not confuse every struggle with hardened rebellion.
Do not use Paul's instruction as an excuse for personal revenge or social cruelty.
And where serious, persistent, unrepentant sin is established within a church, let biblically responsible leaders address it through fair, accountable, restorative discipline.
Do not pretend that continued disobedience is spiritually harmless.
But never stop hoping that the person will return to Christ.
And if the person reading this is the one who has been refusing to repent?
Please hear this.
You do not have to keep defending what is destroying you.
You do not have to spend another night constructing excuses for something your conscience has been warning you about.
You do not have to wait until you feel worthy to come to Jesus.
Come because you need Him.
Come with the truth.
Come with the shame you have been hiding.
Come with the relationship you know must change.
Come with the habits you have been afraid to confess.
Come with the questions, the fear, and the uncertainty about what obedience will cost you.
Do not mistake the pain of surrender for the absence of God's love.
Sometimes obedience means letting go of something you desperately wanted to keep.
But Jesus never promised that following Him would cost us nothing.
He promised something infinitely greater than the things we are called to surrender.
He offers Himself.
And no relationship, pleasure, reputation, or secret sin can give your soul what only Christ can give.
Perhaps this article has brought someone to mind.
Perhaps a church leader needs to remember that biblical correction must be governed by humility and restoration.
Perhaps someone you love needs encouragement to return to Jesus.
And please, do not leave without answering one question in your own heart.
Are you fighting against sin, or have you slowly started making excuses for it?
If God has restored you from a season of rebellion, consider sharing a testimony of His mercy—without exposing private details that could harm you or anyone else.
Your honesty may encourage someone who believes they are too far gone to return.
And if this message convicted you, you do not have to publish your confession for it to be real. Bring it first to God, and seek help from a trustworthy, mature believer when needed.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a crowd around condemnation.
Not to turn another person's failures into entertainment.
But to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, and discipleship.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
It is the opportunity to help make the Gospel known.
Because behind every screen is a human being.
Someone's son.
Someone's daughter.
Someone's husband or wife.
Someone quietly fighting temptation.
Someone who has wandered away.
Someone who is afraid that if people knew the truth, they would never be loved again.
And somewhere among those people may be a person who needs to hear that Jesus still calls sinners to repentance—and still receives those who come to Him.
So let this be the truth we carry with us.
Paul did not tell the church to take sin seriously because grace was too small.
He told the church to take sin seriously because Christ's sacrifice was too precious to treat as meaningless.
And he did not call the church to discipline so that sinners could never return.
He wanted the church to be faithful to the Lord who saves.
There must be room for repentance.
There must be room for accountability.
There must be room for forgiveness.
And when someone genuinely turns back to Christ, there must be room for restoration.
Because the church is not a museum displaying people who have never fallen.
It is a people redeemed by the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
The most heartbreaking tragedy is not that someone fell into sin—it is that they began calling their chains freedom, while the Savior who could set them free was still calling them home.
